description: What if Earth could become our testbed for other worlds? AnalogX is a team passionate about space, science, data, and building bold solutions for future Moon and Mars missions. We bring strengths in research, strategy, UI/UX, and problem-solving. We’re looking for teammates skilled in Python, GIS, web development, AI/ML, data science, or planetary science who want to build something original, useful, and competitive.
summary:
AnalogX, a platform which helps turn ANY Moon or Mars mission briefs into a proper step by step testing campaign on Earth with the help of its embedded Analog AI. A team describes its mission in plain language, and our Analog AI then breaks it down into its risks which the team can review, edit and even prioritize. AnalogX uses those confirmed risks to then retrieve specific and mission required measurements and data from the large data pool, including NASA Planetary datasets, and even recommended multiple Earth Analog sites, each chosen for a specific test.

The risks are then divided into 4 classifications as we acknowledge that no Earth analog can replicate perfect conditions:
 Natural quantifiable
Screen a measurable Earth condition against an explicit test criterion.
Natural representative
Rehearse the procedure in a relevant Earth setting.
Augmented Earth
Add controlled materials or equipment to a field or test yard setup.
Synthetic or digital
Use a chamber, a lab rig or a software simulation. 

An interactive map and detailed sit cards show us what each location can reproduce, its limitations, and when to visit. AnalogX calculates how much of the mission's risk meets the measurable Earth screening criteria and suggests controlled experiments or simulations. If a site becomes unavailable, it recalculates coverage and gives the next best option and updates the roadmap. The final plan tells teams where to go, what to test, how long to spend, and what evidence to collect.
details:
A rover shouldn’t have to reach Mars for its team to discover where its wheels will lose the traction. We built AnalogX to give Moon and Mars mission teams a way to uncover those problems over here, on Earth, while they still have time to change the design. AnalogX turns a mission brief into a full testing campaign and rebuilds that campaign when a site becomes unavailable or falls short. The result is a fully fledged roadmap which will tells teams where to go, what to test, when to do it, and what evidence to actually bring back.

How AnalogX works

1. Analog AI turns a mission description into proper testable risks. A user describes a Moon or Mars mission in simple and plain language. Our embedded AI then drafts a mission profile which identifies risks tied to the destination, equipment, as well as operations. The team then reviews assumptions, edits or removes risks to their needs and wants, and marks which ones are critical. The confirmed risks which determine what data AnalogX looks for (as the mission requires are given, Analog AI analyzes it and looks for only specific data required and extracts it from the large data pool). For a rover traverse, that could mean extracting elevation around the target, calculating the distribution of slopes, and comparing it with Earth terrain measured at a comparable scale.

2. Earth Search finds different sites for different jobs. AnalogX recommends a combination of terrestrial analogs matched to its individual risks. One site might meet a measurable slope criterion, while another which offers dry soil for a wheel-traction rehearsal. The interactive map helps differentiate recommended sites, selected campaign stops, as well as other candidates. Each Site Card explains the site’s strengths and limitations, what to test, how to run the test, the proposed duration and seasonal window, and what still requires a field survey or access confirmation. The Earth catalog contains 63 locations, and a separate terrain search compares 1,102 sampled windows across 24 regions, allowing unusual candidates to surface from the data.

3. Coverage and gaps show exactly what the campaign can test. AnalogX reports the share of weighted risks that meet measurable Earth screening criteria. It separately tracks representative field opportunities, scheduled tests, and recorded results. The four test classes give teams a way to act on each gap:

  • Natural quantifiable uses a measurable Earth condition, such as terrain within an approved slope band.
  • Natural representative uses a relevant setting to rehearse an operation, such as driving on dry soil.
  • Augmented Earth uses controlled equipment or materials, such as an adjustable ramp or a prepared soil bed.
  • Synthetic or digital uses a lab rig, chamber, or software simulation, such as a command-delay replay.

4. The campaign adapts when a site drops out. Removing a stop triggers a fresh coverage calculation. AnalogX identifies the affected risks, reassesses the remaining sites, and proposes another field or controlled test where feasible. In our exemplary mission, the Gale Crater walkthrough, removing Mojave drops quantitative Earth screening from 6 out of 21 to 3 out of 21 weighted risk points. Yungay keeps its traction-rehearsal role, and the rebuilt roadmap adds a Day 2 adjustable-grade rover trial to measure grade, rover tilt, wheel slip, and motor current. The optimizer prioritizes critical risks and works within the team’s field-stop and time limits. The printable roadmap sequences preparation, field and controlled tests, and a final evidence review.

Data, tools, and design decisions

We built the interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and the live data and AI backend with Node.js and the OpenAI API, with the API key held server-side. GeoTIFF and Proj4 help read and align geospatial data. We used NASA MOLA and LRO LOLA for planetary terrain, LRO Diviner for lunar thermal context, NASA POWER for Earth weather and solar data, and Copernicus GLO-30 for Earth elevation. Our Evidence Library exposes sources and limitations so users can trace a recommendation back to the measurements behind it. The public prototype includes bundled evidence and three walkthroughs covering Gale Crater, Nili Fossae, and the lunar south pole. Live AI drafting and live data retrieval run through the separate server.

We considered terrain and mobility, geology and surface materials, ice and drilling, temperature and illumination, dust and power, navigation, communications, and field logistics. We also considered what orbital data can establish. A terrain map can guide a site survey, while wheel sinkage, drill resistance, and equipment wear still require physical measurements. Our Lessons from Real Missions page uses Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity to show how documented incidents could inform earlier traction, low-light power, and wheel-wear tests.

Why it matters

AnalogX’s creative contribution is making an analog part of a campaign that can change. When the evidence changes or a site becomes unavailable, the team can see which risk has reopened and what to do next. That gives mission planners a practical way to focus field time, choose where a lab test is worth the effort, and make better use of NASA data. For future lunar crews and Mars missions, the opportunity is to discover more of the difficult problems here on Earth, where a team can still rerun the test, revise the procedure, or redesign the hardware.
